analysis.one_liner: Ends commercial logging on federal public lands, redirects the money to restoration and worker retraining.
analysis.headline: The bill to end commercial logging on national forests and other federal lands won 35 House sponsors but was never granted a hearing or a vote before Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have shut down the federal program that sells timber from national forests, wildlife refuges, and Bureau of Land Management lands to logging companies, with a two-year phase-out for existing contracts. The bill's own findings say the program costs taxpayers more than it brings in — a 1995 GAO report found only a small fraction of the hundreds of millions spent each year comes back to the Treasury. It would have replaced logging with a restoration program and paid to retrain logging workers who lost their jobs.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who stop funding a logging program the bill says sells public timber below cost; people who use national forests for recreation; and logging workers and their communities, who would get retraining grants, job search and relocation allowances, and hiring preference in the new restoration corps.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits commercial timber sales on National Forest, National Wildlife Refuge, and BLM lands, with a two-year phase-out for existing contracts [S2][S3].

Redirects up to one-third of what the government spends on the logging program toward restoration work — replanting, decommissioning logging roads, reducing fire risk — performed by a new Natural Heritage Restoration Corps that gives hiring preference to displaced timber workers [S3].
Provides worker retraining grants, needs-related payments, and job search and relocation allowances of up to $1,200 each for workers laid off because of the logging phase-out [S2][S3].
Continues revenue-sharing payments to timber counties at the fiscal 1996 level of $125.4 million through 2003, so counties that depend on timber receipts are not cut off [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Logging companies and mills lose access to federal timber (less than 5% of U.S. consumption per the bill's findings, but a larger share regionally), and timber-dependent rural communities face economic disruption, cushioned by retraining and continued county payments.

drawbacks.text: Logging jobs in rural communities would disappear faster than retraining can replace them, and the bill acknowledges this by funding up to $100 million in retraining in the first year and $150 million in the third [S3].

Removing federal timber from the market could shift logging pressure onto private and foreign forests, since federal land supplies less than 5% of U.S. timber consumption but a much larger share in some Pacific Northwest regions [S3].
The restoration and retraining programs are capped at one-third of the current logging subsidy, so the replacement economy would be smaller than the program it replaces [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a straightforward trade: end a program that loses taxpayer money and damages watersheds and habitat, and spend part of the savings helping the workers and counties that depended on it. The strongest objection is that retraining cannot fully replace the culture and economy of timber towns, and the replacement funding is deliberately smaller than the logging program. But the bill's GAO-cited finding that the program returns only a small fraction of what it costs taxpayers is the core of the case for it.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to three committees and five subcommittees, but none of them ever held a hearing or advanced it, and it died when that Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Introduced October 31, 1997 by Rep. Cynthia McKinney with 34 cosponsors, 31 Democrats and 3 Republicans [S4][S5].
Referred the same day to the Agriculture, Resources, and Education and the Workforce committees, then to five subcommittees within a month [S5].
The record shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action after the referrals [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The timber industry kept its access to federal timber sales, and the below-cost federal logging program continued for the rest of the 105th Congress. Rural timber towns also kept the status quo rather than facing the phase-out.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The timber industry and status quo

sides.party_line_note: Support was mostly Democratic — 31 of the 34 cosponsors were Democrats — though three Republicans, including Rep. Jim Leach, signed on; no vote was ever taken to test the full House.

industries.note: The bill ends the federal program that sells public-forest timber to logging companies, which the bill's findings and a GAO report describe as costing taxpayers more than it returns. Its benefit ran at the public's expense, which is the core of the bill's corporate-welfare argument [S3].

Mill jobs and local timber economies would shrink, but the bill cushions the blow with retraining grants, relocation allowances, hiring preference in restoration work, and guaranteed county payments through 2003 [S3].

The bill's findings cite Forest Service data that recreation and tourism generate over 30 times more jobs and income in national forests than commercial logging, and unlogged, restored forests support that economy [S3].
